issues.item: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, these two sensory triggers are hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the self-report. Neither water/flooding nor smoke/fire smell is reflected in the memory or appraisal content, and the formulation links Triggers primarily with Memory and Negative Appraisals. In contrast, the selected appraisals (injustice, low coping, lost meaning) and memories (photographic/snapshot/partial clarity) fit rape, but these two triggers suggest an entirely different trauma context unless a specific trauma narrative supports them. That mismatch is strong enough to question coherence.

vignette:
Meena was a 66-year-old South Asian widow who worked in retail, spending most days on her feet in a bright, busy shop where customers drifted in and out and staff were expected to stay polite no matter what was said to them. Her traumatic experience had occurred years earlier, on an evening when she had been alone with a man she knew only casually, and the details she could recall now came to her in isolated, vivid fragments rather than a continuous story. When she tried to speak about it, she described it as if she were turning over a set of photographs in her mind: a snapshot of the room, a snapshot of his face, a snapshot of her own helplessness. Some moments were so clear to her that she could still picture the arrangement of objects around her, while other parts of the event were blank, leaving her frustrated and ashamed that she could not piece together what had happened from beginning to end. What remained was not a smooth memory but a series of frozen images that returned with a force that made her feel as though she were looking at the scene rather than remembering it.

In the months that followed, Meena noticed that certain moments in ordinary life could bring the event back with startling intensity. If she found herself alone with men, even briefly, her body tightened and her attention narrowed to the nearest exit or doorway. She had come to avoid situations in which she might be isolated with male customers or male coworkers, and at work she arranged herself so that she was usually visible to others, staying near the front of the store or within earshot of the registers. She did not trust herself to handle even small surprises well anymore. When a customer was rude, loud, or behaved in a way she experienced as disrespectful, it struck her not simply as annoyance but as a moral violation that left her feeling unsettled and sickened. She would go quiet, keep her face composed, and continue working, but inside she was left with the sense that the world had become a place where people could behave badly and nothing would be done.

The smell of smoke or fire was especially upsetting. If a customer came in after being near a cigarette, or if something in the store carried a faint burnt odor, Meena would suddenly feel pulled back to the fearful memory in a bodily way she found difficult to explain. She described those moments as if they brought the room around her into sharp, threatening focus, and she would become tense and watchful until the smell passed. At home, she avoided cooking when she could and preferred not to be near anything that might scorch. She knew these reactions made the day harder, but she felt unable to dismiss them.

Over time, Meena's understanding of her life became more bleak. She said that nothing felt meaningful anymore, not in the way it once had after her husband was alive and her life had a clearer shape. She moved through her days because she had to, but without the sense that there was much to look forward to or that her efforts mattered. The unfairness of what had happened to her remained a central wound for her. She spoke with bitterness about how deeply unjust it was, and how nothing had been done about it. That sense of being wronged and left without redress sat heavily with her, especially when she thought about how she had been expected to carry on as though nothing had happened.

She also felt increasingly unable to cope with even slight upset. Small problems at work, minor disagreements, or an unexpected change in routine left her feeling overwhelmed and close to tears. Before the assault, she had considered herself capable and steady, someone who could manage the demands of work and family responsibilities. Now she doubted her ability to deal with ordinary difficulties, and that doubt made her withdraw further into caution. The changes had affected her work life and her relationships there, since she no longer volunteered for tasks that might place her in uncomfortable proximity to men, and she often found herself silently enduring situations that once would not have shaken her.

Meena sought help when she realized how much of her life had become organized around avoiding reminders of what had happened and bracing for the next moment that might unsettle her. What brought her in was not a single dramatic crisis, but the accumulation of those repeated intrusions at work and the growing heaviness of believing that life held little meaning. She was most afraid that she would remain trapped in this state, unable to feel safe around men, unable to tolerate small disturbances, and unable to make peace with what she experienced as an unforgivable injustice. At the same time, she hoped that speaking about it might help her understand why those photographs kept returning so vividly, and whether there was any way to live with the memory without feeling as though it still controlled the shape of her days.
